blocks.text: The opening presents a plural voice that claims to have heard, seen, contemplated, and touched the Word of life. It does not name an apostle, so the “we” should not be assumed to identify one particular kind of witness; readers have understood it in several ways. The stated purpose of this proclamation is fellowship—shared participation with the speakers, the Father, and the Son—rather than automatic approval of an institution or leader.

The chapter joins walking in the light with honest acknowledgment of sin. Its contrast between light and darkness is theological and ethical; it must not be applied to race, disability, mental health, or a person’s social worth. Likewise, confession in verse 9 describes truthfulness before God, not coerced disclosure, compelled testimony, or public shaming.

Verses 3–9 hold several claims together: proclamation aims at fellowship, God is called light, walking in the light is connected with mutual fellowship and cleansing, and confession is paired with forgiveness and cleansing. The “blood of Jesus” language describes cleansing through a death-and-life metaphor in its Christ-centered setting; it should not be used to glorify violence or normalize abuse.

The denial of sin in 1:8–10 should be read alongside 2:1–2 and the later language about those born of God not sinning in 3:4–10. These statements create an interpretive tension, so the chapter’s rejection of claims to be without sin should not be turned into perfectionism, scrupulosity, or mental-health shame.

sections.title: Reading the sin language in context
